newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN boss calls Swiss row with Jews a PR disaster.
newsitem.headline: UN boss calls Swiss row with Jews a PR disaster.

text.p: The new U.N. chief Kofi Annan on Thursday called Switzerland's dispute with Jews over the fate of unclaimed bank accounts a public relations disaster and urged a fair settlement.

"I think the whole issue has been a difficult one for Switzerland and a public relations disaster," he told a news conference when asked if Switzerland's perceived neutrality as host to U.N. European headquarters had been compromised by the row.
"It's unfortunate it has dragged on for so long," he said on his first visit to Geneva as Secretary-General.
"I hope the issue will be resolved quickly and appropriately and equitably to the satisfaction of all parties concerned," Annan said.

He said the U.N. had no plan to move out of Switzerland because of the controversy over claims by Jewish groups that Switzerland profited from millions of dollars in unclaimed bank accounts of victims of Holocaust.
Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti, after meeting Annan in Geneva, conceded that the affair was a fundamental challenge for the future of Switzerland.
"It's a matter of reassessing a history which perhaps has been established only partially, and to do it in the most profound way possible," Cotti told reporters.
"I've already said it a thousand times that this is an absolutely fundamental challenge for our country," he said, adding he had not discussed the affair with Annan.
The dispute has triggered a fierce debate in the Swiss society about latent anti-Semitism and protests abroad.
Partly in response to international criticism, Switzerland set up a commission to investigate allegations that Swiss banks are hoarding the dormant wealth of people Hitler persecuted.

The simmering crisis on Monday claimed the head of the Swiss ambassador to the United States, who resigned after a secret document he wrote calling for "waging war" against Jewish groups and other critics was leaked to the press and caused uproar.

On Wednesday, New York city and state warned Switzerland that they would make it difficult for Swiss banks to do business in New York unless the Swiss created a fund to compensate victims of Holocaust.
Swiss banks say they are already working fast to set up a Holocaust memorial fund and urged New York politicians to study the facts before deciding on a threatened boycott.
Bank spokesmen said they took the boycott threat seriously but were puzzled it came after Swiss businesses and the government last week agreed to a humanitarian fund for victims of Nazi persecution.
In a petition blasting government policy, some 200 leading Swiss intellectuals accused the country's leaders of damaging Switzerland's credibility as a neutral state.

"The standing and credibility of Switzerland as a democratic nation are compromised and imperilled," said the petition, signed by leading Swiss personalities including lawyers, doctors, artists, writers, academics and journalists.

The petition was launched in reaction to remarks by outgoing president Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, who dismissed Jewish groups' calls for quick compensation as "extortion and blackmail" last month. He later apologised after his remarks caused international uproar.
